steps.body: Knowing WHICH WAY you rounded sharpens the check: rounding 68 up to 70 inflates every one of the seven groups, so the estimate sits above the exact answer.
steps.narration: Knowing WHICH WAY you rounded sharpens the check: rounding 68 up to 70 inflates every one of the seven groups, so the estimate sits above the exact answer.

widget.prompt: Rounding 68 up to 70 in 7 × 68 — slide to the size of the overshoot.
widget.lowFeedback: Too low — each of the seven groups gained 2, so the total gained more than that.
widget.highFeedback: Too high — seven groups each gaining 2 adds 14, not more.
widget.successFeedback: 14 — seven groups each inflated by 2, which is exactly why the estimate sits above the exact value.

predict.prompt: Rounding a factor UP — is the estimate above or below?
predict.reveal: Every group was made larger, so the product grew — the estimate overshoots by 7 × 2 = 14.

cml.actionGoal: Name the quantity each step produces, then carry it into the next for g4ms reasonable.
invariants: Each step of a multi-step problem produces a quantity the story never states, and the next step consumes it, which is why naming the intermediate value is what makes g4ms reasonable checkable at all.
misconceptions: Applying the second step to every group instead of the whole, reading "times as many" as "more than", or reporting a quotient when the story needs the partial group rounded up.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: If the second step were applied to each group instead of the total, how far off would the answer be?

widget.prompt: You round 68 UP to 70 when estimating 7 × 68. Will the estimate be above or below the exact answer?

options.label: Above, because each of the 7 groups was made larger
options.feedback: Correct — rounding a factor up inflates every group, so the estimate overshoots by 7 × 2 = 14.

options.label: Below, because rounding always loses something
options.feedback: Rounding UP adds; only rounding down would pull the estimate beneath the exact answer.

options.label: Exactly equal
options.feedback: Changing a factor changes the product, so the estimate cannot match the exact value.

options.label: It is impossible to say
options.feedback: It is predictable: rounding a factor up always raises the product.

widget.prompt: A student computes 7 × 68 − 90 and gets 386. Estimating gives 7 × 70 − 90 = 400. What follows?

options.label: 386 is reasonable — it sits just below the estimate
options.feedback: Correct — rounding 68 up to 70 inflates the estimate slightly, so the exact answer should land just under it.

options.label: 386 is wrong because it is not 400
options.feedback: An estimate is a neighbourhood, not a target; landing 14 away from it is exactly what rounding predicts.

options.label: The estimate is wrong because it is not 386
options.feedback: Rounding deliberately changes the numbers, so a small difference is expected.

options.label: Nothing can be concluded
options.feedback: A great deal can: an answer near 40 or 4,000 would have been caught immediately.
